Confirmed — your theory is exactly right, and I can point at the code:

**`chat.js:50-58`** — the live turn goes through `ask(prompt, { ..., on: e => streamed += e.text })`. That's a streaming callback rendering tokens as they arrive — this is the live path, driven by whatever transport `ask()` uses (the socket).

**`chat.js:28`** — `history.forEach(c => bubble(...))` renders once, from the `history` array passed in as a prop. No subscription, no watcher, no reload-on-write.

**`ask.js:67-70`** (DevBar) — that `history` array comes from `new TaskJSONL({url}).load()` — a plain `fetch` of the `.jsonl` file, done once when you pick a thread.

So: nothing is watching the file. The socket drives the live reply and streams it into the DOM directly; the CLI process (on the server side) appends each turn to `task.jsonl` as a side effect, for persistence; and that file only gets *read* again on a fresh page load / thread switch, via plain `fetch` — the same static-compatible mechanism as everything else in this framework (no build, no runtime server assumptions on the client side, just files).

That's why it doesn't feel like live-reload: it isn't. Live-reload would mean the file write triggers a client refetch. Here the write is just an artifact; the read only happens once, cold, off the JSONL file.
